analysis.one_liner: Requires large companies to audit their automated decision systems for bias, discrimination, and privacy risks.
analysis.headline: The Algorithmic Accountability Act was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in April 2019, never received a hearing markup or floor vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules requiring large companies — those with more than $50 million in annual revenue, data on more than a million people or devices, or data brokers — to study their automated decision systems before and after deployment. These studies would have to examine whether the systems produce inaccurate, unfair, biased, or discriminatory decisions, and how they handle consumers' personal information. Companies would then have to take steps to fix the risks they found. It never advanced beyond its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who are evaluated by automated systems — people applying for jobs or credit, being targeted with ads or pricing, or living under systematic monitoring. The bill would have required companies to document how these systems work, assess whether they discriminate or violate privacy, and take steps to reduce those risks. Because it explicitly preserved state law and allowed state attorneys general to sue, it would also have given state enforcers a tool to act on behalf of residents.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would have required companies to run detailed impact assessments of 'high-risk' automated decision systems — those that could contribute to inaccurate, unfair, biased, or discriminatory decisions, make predictions about sensitive aspects of people's lives such as work performance, health, or economic situation, process sensitive data like race, religion, genetics, or sexuality, or systematically monitor large public spaces [S2][S3].

Assessments would have to describe the system, its training data, and its purpose; weigh its benefits and costs; evaluate risks to privacy and security; assess the risk of biased or discriminatory decisions; and explain what safeguards the company would use to minimize those risks [S2][S3].
The bill would have overridden private contracts, so companies could not write away these obligations in their terms of service, and it expressly preserved state law rather than preempting it [S3].
State attorneys general would have been able to sue on behalf of their residents, alongside FTC enforcement [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies covered by the bill: those with over $50 million in average annual gross receipts, those holding personal information on more than a million consumers or devices, and data brokers that collect and sell information about people who are not their customers. They would bear the cost of conducting impact assessments, consulting outside auditors, and fixing problems found. Part of that cost could be passed to consumers through prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large tech companies and data brokers

drawbacks.text: The assessments' findings would not have had to be public: publication was left to the company's sole discretion [S3], so the main enforcement mechanism would depend on regulators and state attorneys general rather than on consumers seeing the results themselves.

The bill would have imposed real compliance costs on any company over the $50 million revenue threshold or holding data on a million people, including mid-sized firms, and would have required hiring auditors and technology experts; an honest supporter would acknowledge this burden and that it could be passed on to consumers [S3].

Giving the FTC two years to write sweeping rules about automated decision systems and data protection would have been a large delegation of authority to regulators, which critics of expansive FTC rulemaking would object to on the grounds that such rules are difficult for businesses and the agency to implement well [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill asked the companies with the most data and the most consequential algorithms to document and test them for bias and privacy harms before deployment. The costs are real but modest relative to the size of the firms covered, and the biggest design weakness is that the resulting assessments could have remained confidential. On balance it would have shifted accountability over automated decisions toward consumers, at a compliance cost to the data-driven businesses it covered.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Consumer Protection subcommittee in April 2019, and no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke of New York introduced the bill on April 10, 2019 [S1][S5].
The same day it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and the next day to its Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce [S5].
31 House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The full bill text shows the FTC would have been directed to require impact assessments of high-risk automated decision and data systems, with enforcement by the FTC and state attorneys general [S3].
That subcommittee referral was the last action of record; the bill sat with no markup or vote until the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that use large-scale automated decision systems and data brokers benefit, because they never had to conduct bias and privacy assessments or face state enforcement. Consumers evaluated by these systems gained nothing, since the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large data-driven companies and data brokers

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Algorithmic Accountability Act of 2019 in the House.

for.name: 31 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all recorded cosponsors were Democrats.

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or brought it forward; no further action was taken on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Consumer Protection and Commerce subcommittee on April 11, 2019; the bill received no hearing, markup, committee vote, or report before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 31 cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Democratic-controlled committee never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill explicitly covered any company that, as a substantial part of its business, collects personal information about people who are not its customers in order to sell or trade it. It would have required these firms to assess their systems and exposed them to FTC and state attorney general enforcement. Their gain from the bill dying is fewer disclosure obligations and less litigation risk. [S3]

industries.industry: Large technology platforms and data-driven businesses
industries.note: Any firm over $50 million in revenue or holding data on a million consumers or devices would have had to audit its automated decision systems for bias and discrimination and its information systems for privacy and security risks, and fix what it found. These systems influence credit, hiring, pricing, and advertising decisions that shape ordinary people's lives, and the audits could have surfaced practices regulators and consumers currently cannot see. [S2][S3]

The bill directed the FTC to require assessments be conducted, where reasonably possible, in consultation with independent auditors and technology experts, which would have created demand for a new auditing industry. Consumers would have benefited from outside scrutiny of company claims. [S3]
